canonical_statement: The study linked SveDem with Swedish national patient, cause-of-death, and prescribed-drug registers using unique personal identification numbers.

Inverse probability of treatment weighting for the three-level exposure was derived from multinomial logistic regression; weights were truncated at the 99th percentile and covariate balance was defined as standardized mean difference ≤0.1.
Inverse probability of censoring weighting was used in MMSE analyses to address informative attrition from dropout or death.

Weighted linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts estimated exposure-by-time differences in MMSE decline, with additional adjustment for baseline MMSE, care setting and living/care variables, and an anti-dementia-drug-by-time interaction.

IPTW-weighted Cox regression estimated 3-year cause-specific hazard ratios; competing non-death outcomes were also evaluated with Fine–Gray models, and weighted Aalen–Johansen estimates provided cumulative incidence, risk differences, and restricted mean time lost over 5 years.

Sensitivity analyses changed the non-user comparator, excluded recent anticoagulant discontinuers, restricted diagnoses to 2013–2020, modeled non-linear or transformed MMSE trajectories, and used per-protocol exposure analyses for clinical outcomes.
After IPTW, all included covariates were balanced across pairwise exposure comparisons with standardized mean differences no greater than 0.1.
NOAC users had a 0.23-point/year slower MMSE decline than anticoagulant non-users.

canonical_statement: The NOAC-versus-warfarin associations were generally robust across sensitivity analyses, whereas comparisons with anticoagulant non-users varied more with comparator definition.

Using antiplatelet users as the reference group, both warfarin and NOAC use were associated with slower cognitive decline, and protective associations for ischaemic stroke/systemic embolism were stronger.
Excluding recent anticoagulant discontinuers or restricting AD diagnoses to 2013–2020 produced cognitive and clinical results aligned with the main analysis.
Per-protocol analyses of clinical outcomes were consistent with the primary intention-to-treat analysis, with a larger estimated mortality association.
The study used ongoing anticoagulant exposure at the AD diagnosis index date rather than a new-user design because treatment was usually initiated before AD diagnosis.

Residual or unmeasured confounding cannot be excluded despite IPTW because frailty, functional status, clinical judgment, patient preference, and medication uptake were not fully captured in registry data.
Anticoagulant exposure was estimated from dispensing data and assumed constant in the primary analysis despite treatment changes during follow-up.
MMSE assessments came from routine clinical practice, producing variable numbers and timing of measurements and likely non-random attrition, which the authors addressed with IPCW.
Register-based diagnosis outcomes are subject to some misclassification, although the authors expected this to be largely non-differential across anticoagulant groups.
The study lacked power to evaluate individual NOAC agents and did not examine dementia subtypes other than AD and mixed AD dementia.

The authors concluded that NOAC use in patients with AF and AD was associated with modestly slower cognitive decline and a more favorable effectiveness and safety profile than warfarin or no anticoagulation.
The authors cautioned that anticoagulation decisions should remain primarily guided by stroke prevention rather than anticipated cognitive benefit while further cognitive-outcome evidence is awaited.
